Yesterday afternoon you left with a team, a dataset, three questions and one rough figure.

Today you find out which of your three questions the data can actually answer. There is no new
Python in the next two days and there is not meant to be, since every method this project needs is
one you have already written (you wrote the split-apply-combine sentence in 5a, again in that
afternoon's colab, and three more times in the evening's practice). What is new is that nobody is
going to tell you which one to reach for.

## The shape of the day

| {{< fa clock title="A clock" >}} When | {{< fa laptop-code title="A laptop with on-screen code" >}} What |
|------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 10:00 to 11:30   | Choose the question. Steps 1 and 2, import and explore.            |
| **11:30**        | **Checkpoint 1** |
| 11:30 to 12:00   | Begin Step 3, clean. |
| 12:00 to 1:00    | Lunch |
| 1:00 to 2:30     | Steps 3 to 6: clean, filter, sort, transform. |
| **2:30**         | **Checkpoint 2** |
| 2:30 to 4:30     | Steps 7 to 9: group, aggregate, join or reshape. One real figure. |
| **4:30**         | **Checkpoint 3** |

Nothing is handed in today. The checkpoints exist so that a team which is stuck finds out on
Thursday, while there is still a day to spend, rather than on Friday at noon.

## The three checkpoints

### Checkpoint 1, about 11:30. One question, and the data in front of you

By late morning your notebook should hold:

- **One question**, chosen from the three questions you wrote yesterday, written near the top of
  the notebook in a complete sentence, with your actual column names in it.
- A sentence saying **why the other two questions were set aside**. Usually the data cannot answer
  them, and writing down why is worth the minute it takes.
- **Step 1, Import**, under its own heading: the read, the URL, and one sentence on what one row
  represents.
- **Step 2, Explore**, under its own heading: `.shape`, `.dtypes`, `.isnull().sum()`, `.describe()`,
  and a written note on anything surprising.

If you are still choosing between datasets at 11:30, stop choosing and take whichever one loaded
cleanly. A dull dataset you can open beats an exciting one you cannot.

### Checkpoint 2, about 2:30. The data is in the shape the question needs

By mid afternoon, steps 3 to 6 should be done and written up:

- **Step 3, Clean.** What was missing, what you did about it, and how many rows that cost you.
  If the file arrived clean, say so under the heading and move on. Saying so is the step done
  properly.
- **Step 4, Filter.** Which rows the question is about, and which it is not.
- **Step 5, Sort.** Even if sorting is only how you looked at the result.
- **Step 6, Transform.** Any column you derived, with the reason you needed it.

The test is whether you can point at one DataFrame and say, in a sentence, what question that
table is about. The amount of code it took to get there does not matter.

### Checkpoint 3, 4:30. The analysis is finished

By the end of the day the answer should exist, even if it is ugly:

- **Steps 7 and 8, Group and Aggregate.** The split, apply and combine that produces the numbers
  your claim rests on, with the counts each group is built from.
- **Step 9, Join or Reshape.** If your project uses a single table and needs neither, write that
  under the heading and move on.
- **One real figure**, with axis labels, that shows the thing you are going to claim.
- **One sentence** in markdown saying what you found.

The one-sentence finding is the point of the whole exercise. Tomorrow morning is for making it
presentable, and there is nothing to make presentable until you have written it down.

## If you are behind at a checkpoint

Being behind at a checkpoint is normal on a two-day project. The fix is almost never to work
faster.

- **Behind at Checkpoint 1.** The dataset is the problem. Change it. Go back to the five tests in
  the [project kickoff](interactive-sessions/7d_project_kickoff.qmd) and pick something that
  passes all five tests. You will lose an hour and save a day.
- **Behind at Checkpoint 2.** The question is too big. Narrow it, usually by dropping a
  comparison: two groups instead of six, one year instead of a decade.
- **Behind at Checkpoint 3.** Stop adding and start writing. A finished small analysis presents
  well. An unfinished large one does not.

Come and find me at any of the three checkpoints.

## End-of-day practice

There is no end-of-day activity today. The project is the work.

If you have twenty minutes tonight, read your own notebook from the top as though somebody else
wrote it, and fix every place where you cannot tell what a cell was for. You will find more than you
expect. I always do.
